oneIdea: You are given a few exact data points and need a smooth curve that passes through every one of them. A polynomial can do it, and Lagrange and Newton are two ways of writing the same polynomial. But one high-degree polynomial can swing wildly between points, so the practical fix is many small cubic pieces: a spline.
goals: Say the difference between interpolation (exact data, curve hits every point) and regression (noisy data, curve follows the trend).
Explain why \(n+1\) points fix exactly one polynomial of degree \(\le n\).
Build the Lagrange and Newton polynomials through 3 points by hand and use them to estimate a value.
Explain why a single high-degree polynomial oscillates (Runge's phenomenon) and what a spline does differently.
Use MATLAB's interp1 to interpolate a data table.

intro.idea: Interpolation means estimating between known points. The data are trusted, so the curve must go through them.
intro.mistake: Using interpolation on noisy measurements. If the data contain errors, forcing the curve through every point also fits the errors; use regression (Module 3) instead.

check.q: A table of exact values of a physical constant at several temperatures is given. Which tool fits?
check.why: Exact data means the curve should pass through every point, which is interpolation. Regression is for noisy measurements.

poly.idea: Given \(n+1\) points there is exactly one polynomial of degree \(\le n\) through them. Lagrange and Newton are different ways of writing that same polynomial.
poly.mistake: Thinking Lagrange and Newton give different curves. They give the same polynomial, only written differently.

check.q: How many points are needed to determine a unique parabola (degree 2)?
check.why: Degree \(n\) needs \(n+1\) points, so a parabola needs 3.

lagrange.idea: Build one small polynomial \(L_i\) per data point that equals 1 at its own point and 0 at all the others, then add them up weighted by the \(y\)-values.
lagrange.mistake: Using the y-values inside \(L_i\). The \(L_i\) use only the \(x\)-values; the \(y\)-values are multiplied in afterwards.

check.q: For nodes \(x=1,2,3\), what is \(L_1(2)\) (the basis polynomial belonging to the node \(x=1\), evaluated at \(x=2\))?
check.why: \(L_i\) is 1 at its own node and 0 at every other node. Here \(x=2\) is a different node from \(x=1\), so the value is 0.

newton.idea: Start with a constant, then add one new term per data point. Each new term is a divided difference times the product of the earlier \((x-x_j)\) factors, so adding a point never forces you to start over.
newton.mistake: Dividing by the wrong gap. Each divided difference divides by the difference of the outermost \(x\)-values of that column, not by the neighbouring gap.

check.q: You add a fourth point to a Newton polynomial built from three. What must you do?
opts: Add one new term using one new divided difference
check.why: This is the main advantage of Newton's form: the old terms stay, and one new term is added.

runge.idea: More points and a higher degree do not mean a better curve. Between the points a high-degree polynomial can oscillate strongly, especially near the ends.
runge.mistake: Believing that passing through all the points means being close to the true function in between.

check.q: You have 15 equally spaced data points. Which is the safer interpolation?
check.why: A single high-degree polynomial tends to oscillate (Runge's phenomenon). Low-degree pieces joined smoothly avoid this.

spline.idea: Use many low-degree pieces, one per interval, and force neighbouring pieces to join smoothly. The cubic spline is the standard choice.
spline.mistake: Treating a spline as one formula. It is a different cubic on each interval, joined so that slope and curvature agree at the joints.

check.q: What does a cubic spline match at each interior joint between two pieces?
check.why: Matching value, first derivative and second derivative makes the curve look smooth, with no corner and no sudden change in bending.

matlab.idea: In practice you call a built-in. interp1 does linear, spline and other interpolation of a data table.
matlab.mistake: Passing the query points outside the data range and trusting the answer. MATLAB returns NaN or extrapolates, depending on the option.

check.q: Which call gives a smooth cubic spline through the data?
check.why: 'spline' selects cubic spline interpolation; 'linear' joins points with straight segments; polyfit is regression.
